results.title: Feedback-Driven Pseudo-Label Reliability Assessment: Redefining Thresholding for Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation
results.content:
Title: Feedback-Driven Pseudo-Label Reliability Assessment: Redefining Thresholding for Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation
Instead of relying on static confidence thresholds, ENCORE estimates class-wise true-positive confidence within the unlabeled dataset and continuously adjusts thresholds based on the model’s response to different levels of pseudo-label filtering. Our fully automated thresholding strategy, implemented within ENCORE, eliminates a major hyperparameter in pseudo-supervision while significantly enhancing semi-supervised learning performance across different pseudo-labeling frameworks. Our objective is to train a model ℳS⁢(⋅,θ)subscriptℳ𝑆⋅𝜃\mathcal{M}\_{S}(\cdot,\theta)caligraphic\_M start\_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic\_S end\_POSTSUBSCRIPT ( ⋅ , italic\_θ ) that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve segmentation performance on unseen samples. ACT further improves pseudo-label selection by iteratively evaluating different threshold levels using assessor networks and selecting the optimal threshold based on segmentation performance on labeled data. Unlike conventional methods with fixed confidence thresholds, ENCORE continuously adapts its thresholding strategy based on real-time feedback, preventing over- or under-filtering of pseudo-labels and enhancing segmentation accuracy. By integrating CAC and ACT, our approach dynamically calibrates confidence levels and optimally selects pseudo-labels, leading to more reliable supervision and improved segmentation performance. The class-wise reliability indicator R𝑅Ritalic\_R is computed once using a network trained solely on labeled images and is set as the initial class-wise confidence threshold in the first iteration of semi-supervised learning. This enables a more adaptive pseudo-label selection strategy, ensuring that confidence thresholds are class-specific rather than globally fixed, thereby reducing bias toward high-confidence classes and improving segmentation performance across all classes. The segmentation performance of each assessor is then evaluated on the labeled batch using the Dice metric, and the threshold controller that yields the highest Dice score is selected as the optimal controller for pseudo-label filtering in the next student model training cycle:. This approach adaptively refines threshold controllers, allowing the model to dynamically adjust confidence filtering in response to its learning progression, improving pseudo-label reliability throughout training. As expected, performance gains with ENCORE were most pronounced in extreme low-data settings (one and two labeled volumes); however, improvements remained consistently high across different semi-supervised learning frameworks. In this paper, we introduced Ensemble-of-Confidence Reinforcement (ENCORE), a dynamic feedback-driven pseudo-label thresholding strategy for semi-supervised semantic segmentation. Unlike conventional methods that rely on a fixed confidence threshold, ENCORE adaptively refines class-wise pseudo-label selection by leveraging a feedback mechanism.

results.title: Image-Level Uncertainty in Pseudo-Label Selection for Semi-Supervised Segmentation
results.content: Image-Level Uncertainty in Pseudo-Label Selection for Semi-Supervised Segmentation - PMC. However, to our knowledge, current literature lacks an analysis of image-level confidence and uncertainty values to select images for pseudo-labeling for segmentation. 1) We adapt the confidence and image thresholding technique in [6] to create image-level confidence and uncertainty measures to select images for pseudo-labeling in binary segmentation. 3) We show the ability of the relationship between image-level uncertainty and performance on labeled data in indicating overall model performance on a hold out test set on 3 separate digital histopathology datasets. We begin with examining the correlations between image-level model performance on the labeled dataset, referenced in Table I as the training dice, and the associated uncertainty and confidence measures. Thus, the magnitude and direction of these correlation for the labeled dataset is the best proxy for how the model would behave on the unlabeled data, and so indicate the model’s usefulness in pseudo-label image selection. In line with [6], we set minimum confidence and maximum uncertainty thresholds to select which unlabeled images to pseudo-label and use for training for each dataset. This weighting has the effect of creating an adaptive, gradual threshold which weights each image’s pseudo-labels in relation to the model’s certainty about the image and in relation to the uncertainty of the trained dataset. This correlation, though in the minority of the randomly initialized runs, does demonstrate an instance where the image-level confidence and uncertainty values from a model are not useful in selecting pseudo-labels, since minimizing image-level uncertainty results in selecting images with less accurate pseudo-labels. Table II shows that most pseudo-label selection methods gives a statistically significant boost to the model’s test performance for EoE, but this occurs for all models, regardless of whether the correlation is as expected. For CoNSeP, using the minimum 25% entropy pseudo-labels worsened the model performance for the poorly trained seeds, whereas for the models with the expected correlations were not negatively impacted in a significant way by any of the pseudo-label weightings. Before using pseudo-labeling, examining the correlations between certainty metrics and a model’s performance on labeled imagery may help indicate whether a model’s uncertainty about an image is informative. The proposed approach adapts image-level confidence and uncertainty measures for segmentation pseudo-labeling on digital pathology datasets.

Train a neural network on labeled data and unlabeled data using the weighted loss function, in which α(t) is slowly increasing as the number of epochs increases. Pick up the class which has maximum predicted probability by the neural network as pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data. Use pseudo-labels as if they are true labels, train labeled and unlabeled data simultaneously. The most common method used in data-based machine fault detection is the FFT or Fast Fourier transform³. A number of tests were done with different splitting of labeled and unlabeled data and a varying number of labeled data. For each test, only one type of fault is observed during training, and furthermore, only a subset of the observed data is labeled.
